body:
Geographical extent

Gujarat's eastern tribal belt extends through the hilly and forested areas near its eastern boundaries. It stretches broadly from the northern Aravalli region through the eastern districts of Central Gujarat to the forested hills of South Gujarat.

Important districts associated with this belt include Banaskantha, Sabarkantha, Aravalli, Mahisagar, Dahod, Panchmahal, Chhota Udepur, Narmada, Tapi, Dang, Navsari and Valsad, among others.

The belt is a broad cultural and geographical region rather than a single administrative unit. Tribal communities also inhabit areas outside eastern Gujarat.

Important tribal communities

Gujarat's tribal population consists of several communities with distinct languages, dialects, social customs, occupations and cultural practices.

CommunityRepresentative geographical associations
BhilNorthern and eastern Gujarat, including Dahod and Panchmahal
Rathwa or RathvaChhota Udepur and adjoining areas
GamitTapi, Surat and adjoining southern tribal areas
ChaudhariTapi, Surat and adjoining areas
DhodiaValsad, Navsari and adjoining southern areas
Kokna or KuknaDang, Navsari and Valsad
Warli or VarliSouthern Gujarat, especially Valsad and adjoining areas
VasavaNarmada and adjoining eastern and southern areas
KotwaliaForested areas of South Gujarat

These are representative geographical associations, not exclusive boundaries of residence. Migration, employment and settlement patterns have spread communities beyond their traditional areas.

Agriculture and forest-based livelihoods

Agriculture is an important occupation among tribal communities of eastern Gujarat. Depending on rainfall, soil, irrigation and locality, households cultivate crops such as maize, rice, millets and pulses.

Forests also contribute to household consumption and income through minor forest produce. Examples include mahua flowers, tendu or timru leaves, bamboo and locally available edible forest products.

The importance of forests does not mean that all tribal communities depend exclusively on hunting or gathering. Agriculture, wage employment, livestock rearing, crafts, trade and modern occupations also form part of tribal livelihoods.

Kotwalia bamboo crafts

The Kotwalia community is particularly associated with traditional bamboo work. Bamboo is used to prepare baskets, winnowing fans, trays, brooms and other articles required in agricultural and domestic life.

This craft illustrates a direct relationship between forest resources, traditional knowledge, useful household objects and income generation.

The traditional haat

A haat is a periodic local market, commonly organised on a particular day of the week. Haats are especially significant in tribal and rural areas.

Farmers and artisans sell grains, vegetables, livestock, bamboo articles, utensils, clothing and ornaments. People also purchase necessary household goods, meet relatives and exchange information.

The haat is therefore both an economic institution and a centre of community interaction. A haat differs from a mela because it is primarily a periodic market, whereas a mela is generally a larger gathering associated with a festival, religious occasion or special cultural event.

Traditional ecological knowledge

Knowledge of seasonal crops, forest products, water sources and locally available construction materials is transmitted through everyday work and community experience. Such knowledge contributes to cultural continuity.

Changes in forest access, land use, migration, agricultural methods and market demand influence traditional livelihoods. Cultural heritage may therefore adapt without disappearing completely.

Tribal communities outside the eastern belt

The Siddi community of Gujarat, associated with African ancestry, has settlements in the Gir region of Saurashtra, including Jambur. Its cultural traditions include Dhamal.

The Siddi example demonstrates that Gujarat's tribal cultural diversity cannot be identified exclusively with its eastern forested belt.

Prelims focus

  • Rathwas are particularly associated with Chhota Udepur.
  • Gamits and Chaudharis are associated with the southern tribal belt.
  • Kotwalias are traditionally associated with bamboo crafts.
  • A haat is a periodic local market.
  • Siddis are associated with Jambur and the Gir region of Saurashtra.
  • Trap: Not all tribal communities of Gujarat live in the eastern belt or depend exclusively on forest produce.

[References: Government of Gujarat, Tribal Development Department, Annual Report on Administration of Scheduled Areas 2017-18, section 1.4; Tribal Development Department, Tribal Development Initiatives, community distribution table; Tribal Development Department, publication dated 25 May 2022, section 7.3, Kotwalia; District Chhota Udepur, Government of Gujarat, Culture and Heritage; Gujarat Forest Department, Gir Book, 2023, section 7.2, p. 23. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Eastern Tribal Belt: Communities, Livelihoods and Forest-Based Heritage

body:
Pithora painting

Pithora painting is an important ritual painting tradition associated particularly with the Rathwa community of eastern Gujarat, especially Chhota Udepur and adjoining areas.

The paintings are traditionally created on the interior walls of houses in connection with religious beliefs, vows and ceremonies associated with Baba Pithora. They are not merely decorative paintings; they have a religious and social purpose within the community.

Traditional compositions frequently contain rows of horses, together with human figures, animals, natural elements and scenes connected with community life and religious narratives.

Horses are particularly characteristic of the Pithora tradition. Traditional Pithora painters are known as Lakharas.

The transfer of Pithora painting to paper, canvas and other commercial surfaces has enabled the tradition to reach wider audiences. Nevertheless, its original association with household walls and ritual ceremonies remains important for understanding its cultural identity.

Warli painting

Warli painting is associated with the Warli community of the western Indian tribal region, particularly Maharashtra and adjoining parts of southern Gujarat.

Traditional Warli paintings are characterised by simple geometrical human and animal figures, commonly executed in white against an earthen background. Circles, triangles and lines represent people, animals, trees and activities such as farming, dancing and community gatherings.

Unlike the colourful compositions and prominent horses of Pithora painting, Warli painting is particularly recognisable through its simplified geometrical forms and traditional contrast between white pigment and an earthen surface.

Pithora is particularly associated with Rathwa ritual traditions, whereas Warli painting is associated with the Warli community. Both are tribal art traditions, but their characteristic forms, community associations and ceremonial contexts differ.

Traditional tribal dress and ornaments

Traditional attire in Gujarat's tribal regions varies considerably between communities. Garments, jewellery, head coverings, body decoration and embroidery can express community identity and mark important occasions.

Traditional silver jewellery, including necklaces, bangles, nose ornaments and anklets, is particularly visible during community fairs and ceremonies. Tattooing has also been a traditional practice among several tribal communities, including Rathwas.

Men and women often wear distinctive ceremonial clothing during festivals and marriages. Such clothing differs from everyday working garments and should not be treated as the compulsory dress of an entire community.

Ecological significance of tribal art and crafts

Traditional art frequently represents animals, agricultural activities, forests, seasonal cycles and community celebrations. These subjects reflect the environment and occupations familiar to the artists.

Bamboo articles, earthen wall paintings and locally produced ornaments demonstrate how cultural traditions make use of available resources. At the same time, the religious meaning of these objects cannot be explained by environmental resources alone.

Prelims focus

  • Pithora painting is particularly associated with the Rathwas of Chhota Udepur.
  • Its traditional setting is the interior walls of houses.
  • Horses are characteristic motifs in Pithora painting.
  • Lakharas are traditional Pithora painters.
  • Warli painting is recognisable through geometrical figures and traditionally white pigment on an earthen background.
  • Trap: Warli painting is not confined exclusively to Maharashtra; its cultural region also extends into southern Gujarat.

[References: District Chhota Udepur, Government of Gujarat, Culture and Heritage; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Press Information Bureau, 2023 profile of Pithora artist Paresh Rathwa; Government of Gujarat, Craft of Gujarat, One District One Product list, Warli craft entries for Navsari; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9-12; Gujarat Tourism, Kavant Fair, Dang Darbar and Chitra Vichitra Fair. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Tribal Ritual Art, Dress and Cultural Traditions

body:
Importance of tribal fairs

Tribal fairs in Gujarat bring together religious observances, seasonal celebrations, community relationships, traditional clothing, music, crafts and local commerce.

They provide opportunities for communities from different villages to gather, exchange goods, renew social relationships and participate in shared cultural traditions. Several important tribal fairs take place around Holi or after the agricultural harvest.

Dang Darbar

Dang Darbar is held at Ahwa in Dang district, generally shortly before Holi.

The celebration has a historical association with gatherings of tribal rulers and village chiefs during British rule. The tradition continues as an important cultural event of the region, bringing together local tribal communities.

Traditional attire, silver ornaments, music, dancing and community gatherings are prominent features. Dang Darbar reflects both the political history and the living cultural heritage of the Dangs.

Kavant Fair

Kavant, also written as Kawant or Kavantu, is situated in Chhota Udepur district. Its traditional Gher Mela is particularly associated with the Rathwa community and takes place around the period following Holi.

The fair provides an opportunity for community gatherings, exchange of goods, celebration, traditional clothing and social interaction. Rathwa cultural identity is expressed through the participants' distinctive ceremonial dress and ornaments.

Chitra Vichitra Fair

Chitra Vichitra Fair is held near Gunbhakhari village in Poshina taluka of Sabarkantha district, close to the Rajasthan border.

The fair takes place approximately a fortnight after Holi, around the new moon. It is associated with the Triveni Sangam, the confluence of the Sabarmati, Akul and Vyakul rivers.

Traditional observances include remembrance of deceased family members, followed by community celebrations and social gatherings. The fair also provides opportunities for meeting prospective marriage partners.

Shamlaji Fair

Shamlaji is an important pilgrimage centre situated in Aravalli district. Its traditional fair is associated with Kartik Purnima and attracts pilgrims, including members of tribal communities from surrounding areas.

The fair combines religious pilgrimage with commerce and social interaction. Its religious calendar distinguishes it from the tribal fairs associated with Holi.

Comparing the major tribal fairs

FairLocationTraditional timingPrincipal association
Dang DarbarAhwa, DangBefore HoliHistorical gatherings of tribal rulers and chiefs
Kavant FairChhota UdepurAfter HoliRathwa community and Gher Mela
Chitra VichitraGunbhakhari, SabarkanthaAbout a fortnight after HoliAncestor remembrance and river confluence
Shamlaji FairAravalliKartik PurnimaReligious pilgrimage and tribal participation

The timing of these fairs follows traditional religious or seasonal calendars. Their corresponding Gregorian calendar dates vary from year to year.

Comparing Gujarat's cultural landscapes

Kutch illustrates adaptation to aridity, salinity and pastoral grasslands through millet-based food, salt production, animal husbandry, bhunga dwellings and textile crafts. Rann Utsav connects these traditions with organised cultural tourism.

Saurashtra combines dryland agriculture and pastoral traditions with fishing, maritime occupations and coastal pilgrimage. Kathiawadi cuisine, Tarnetar Fair and Madhavpur Fair are distinctive regional associations.

The eastern tribal belt illustrates relationships between agriculture, forests, bamboo crafts, ritual art and community markets. Rathwa Pithora painting, Kotwalia bamboo work, Dang Darbar, Kavant Fair and Chitra Vichitra Fair represent different aspects of this heritage.

Across these landscapes, food traditions reflect agricultural conditions and community customs. Dress and ornaments express regional, ceremonial and community identities. Crafts and festivals preserve traditional knowledge while also supporting commerce and livelihoods.

Prelims focus

  • Dang Darbar is held at Ahwa before Holi.
  • Kavant Fair is particularly associated with the Rathwa community.
  • Chitra Vichitra Fair is held at Gunbhakhari in Sabarkantha.
  • Its Triveni Sangam consists of the Sabarmati, Akul and Vyakul rivers.
  • Shamlaji Fair is associated with Kartik Purnima.
  • Trap: Rann Utsav is associated with the Great Rann of Kutch and is distinct from the traditional tribal fairs of eastern Gujarat.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, Heritage of India, pp. 3-4; District Chhota Udepur, Government of Gujarat, Culture and Heritage; Gujarat Tourism, Dang Darbar, Kavant Fair, Chitra Vichitra Fair, Rann Utsav, Madhavpur Fair and Tarnetar Fair; Government of Gujarat, Tribal Development Department, Annual Report on Administration of Scheduled Areas 2017-18, section 1.4. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]
